# Find the Integer Added to Array I.

@example Adding 3 gives 7, 3 and 10, which nums2 holds in another order.
[4,0,7]
[3,10,7]
=> 3

@example Subtracting 10 turns 12, 15, 12 into 2, 5, 2: the value 2 twice and 5 once, as in nums2.
[12,15,12]
[5,2,2]
=> -10

@example The two arrays hold the same values, only in the other order, so nothing was added.
[6,9]
[9,6]
=> 0

# A single element, with the largest shift up and down.
[0]
[1000]
=> 1000

[1000]
[0]
=> -1000

# The largest shift with several elements.
[0,0,0,0]
[1000,1000,1000,1000]
=> 1000

# All values equal.
[5,5,5,5,5]
[2,2,2,2,2]
=> -3

# Duplicates, and no position of nums2 holds nums1[i] + x.
[3,1,3,2]
[4,5,3,5]
=> 2

# Nothing added, but the order differs, so nums2[0] - nums1[0] is not 0.
[7,1,4,1]
[1,4,1,7]
=> 0

# The smallest of nums2 minus the largest of nums1 would give -8.
[1,10]
[11,2]
=> 1

# A negative shift, shuffled: the answer is -15, not 15.
[20,30,25]
[10,5,15]
=> -15

# Both bounds in nums1 leave room only for 0.
[1000,0,500]
[0,500,1000]
=> 0

# Far-apart values moved up by 1.
[999,0,1]
[1,2,1000]
=> 1

# Random cases from gen.c (lc check --regen makes them).
@gen 1 small
[4,4,7,6,6,6,6]
[3,1,3,4,3,1,3]
=> -3

@gen 2 small
[3,7,7,3,5]
[4,0,2,4,0]
=> -3

@gen 3 small
[0,0,0,1,0,9,0,0]
[9,0,0,0,0,1,0,0]
=> 0

@gen 4 small
[0,10,6,4]
[10,4,0,6]
=> 0

@gen 5 small
[9,10,10,9,10,10]
[0,0,1,1,1,1]
=> -9

@gen 6 small
[7,7]
[1,1]
=> -6
